# M365 GCC is listed at Class D (High), and lost FedRAMP Certified status in July 2026

## 1. Constraint

The FedRAMP Marketplace listing for **Microsoft 365 Government Community Cloud
& Supporting Services**, package ID **`MSO365MTA`**, read directly from
`fedramp.gov/marketplace` on 9 September 2026:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Class** | **Class D (High)** |
| **Status** | **FedRAMP In Process** — as of 2026-07-20 |
| Phase | Initial Implementation |
| Certification Type / Path | Rev5 / Agency |
| **Authorizations** | **0** |
| Certified since | **N/A** |

The listing's own certification history records how it reached that state:

- **2026-07-01** — status changed **from FedRAMP Certified** to *Agency
  Authorization In Process*
- **2026-07-20** — *Agency Review* → **FedRAMP In Process**

M365 GCC therefore **lost certified status in July 2026** and is mid-
recertification under Rev5 at Class D. This is a live transition, not a stale
record.

## 2. What this overturns

**"GCC-Moderate" is wrong about the level, not merely unqualified.** The
standing corpus position — carried in B.1 §0 and repeated across nine
documents — was that the level is *contested* because Microsoft's own
documentation disagrees with itself, and that no document should assert one
until the Marketplace was read. The Marketplace has now been read. It says
**High**. Any document reasoning from "GCC = Moderate" has the level wrong.

**The prior description of the listing was outdated.** The 2026-09-04
Requirements Register states GCC is listed as *"Office 365
(Commercial)/Multitenant"*. It is not. It is listed under its own name, with a
separate listing for **Microsoft 365 Government Community Cloud-High**.

**The Marketplace itself equates Class D with High.** Its filter facets render
*"Class D (High)"*, *"Class C (Moderate)"*, *"Class B (Low)"* and *"Class A
(Pilot)"*. That is FedRAMP's own UI mapping the 2026 classes onto the legacy
impact levels, notwithstanding FedRAMP's separate caution that the classes are
not one-for-one replacements. Cite the class, and note the parenthetical is
FedRAMP's rendering rather than an equivalence this substrate asserts.

**`marketplace.fedramp.gov` is deprecated** and permanently redirects to
`fedramp.gov/marketplace`. That is why every automated retrieval attempt
returned nothing: the recorded URL no longer serves the listing.

## 3. An unresolved tension this creates

The listing's vendor-supplied service description states:

> "M365 GCC leverages **Azure Government** as the IaaS/PaaS for the underlying
> infrastructure and hardware. Therefore, M365 GCC relies on Azure
> Government-inherited services."

[ADR-141](../adr/adr-141-fedramp-20x-boundary-model-refinement.qmd) and
[the 20x commercial-feature whitepaper](../customer-documents/whitepapers/fedramp-20x-and-the-commercial-feature-gap.qmd)
both cite Microsoft's M365 enterprise docset (p.755) for GCC pairing with
**Azure Commercial**, while GCC High and DoD pair with Azure Government.

These are most likely **true at different layers** — the docset statement is
about Entra ID tenant pairing on the identity plane; the Marketplace statement
is about IaaS/PaaS hosting — and the corpus states the docset claim in identity
terms. But that reconciliation is inference, not evidence, and neither source
is authoritative for the other's layer: FedRAMP explicitly disclaims
vendor-submitted content, and the M365 docset carries no FedRAMP or hosting
architecture material.

**Do not resolve this by swapping one for the other.** Until a source that
speaks to both layers is found, documents should state the layer they mean and
cite accordingly.

## 4. What is still open

- **The GCC-High listing's class was not captured.** A separate *Microsoft 365
  Government Community Cloud-High* listing exists; its class, status and
  authorization count were not read. If GCC is Class D, the natural question is
  what distinguishes GCC High under the 2026 classes, and that is unanswered
  here.
- **Whether a legacy certified listing persists** alongside the in-process one,
  which would explain how agencies operate GCC today against an offering
  showing zero authorizations.
- The Azure Commercial / Azure Government layer question in §3.

## 5. Verification boundary

Every value in §1 was read from the product page for `MSO365MTA` in a browser,
not inferred. The service description quoted in §3 is **vendor-submitted**, and
the Marketplace carries an explicit disclaimer that FedRAMP does not review or
endorse it. A Marketplace listing is also a snapshot of a moving process — this
one changed twice in July 2026 — so the status and class should be re-read
before either is used in an ATO narrative or a funding decision.
